title: Is your game juicy enough? (summary of Jonasson & Purho, Juice it or lose it)
label: developer
claim: Juice = maximum output for minimum input; demo is a Breakout clone made lively by tweening, squash/stretch, sound; they claim graphics matter less than responsiveness. Secondhand summary, no data; presenters' opinion.

title: Indies resist the urge to juice it or lose it (Folmer Kelly counter-talk, GDC Europe)
label: snippet
claim: Counter-talk: polish makes a game feel alive but players may lose immersion; juice is not free.

title: How does juicy game feedback motivate? Testing curiosity, competence, and effectance (Kao et al., CHI 2024)
label: research
claim: Preregistered, 1,699 participants, action RPG, 2x2+control. Success-dependent feedback enhanced all motives; amplification (bigger feedback) unexpectedly REDUCED them, possibly undermining sense of control; curiosity the strongest predictor of enjoyment and only predictor of playtime; uncertain success affords curiosity.

title: Game feel (Swink definition)
label: snippet
claim: Swink: real-time control of virtual objects in a simulated space, with interactions emphasised by polish; six areas input, response, context, polish, metaphor, rules. Defined around an avatar under real-time control.

title: Animation and motion (web.dev) / WCAG 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions
label: practitioner
claim: prefers-reduced-motion is a sufficient technique for WCAG 2.3.3 (AAA); advice that non-essential animation can default to reduced; offer pause controls. Motion triggered by interaction is the target.

title: Dreamlight Valley accessibility (screen shake and flash toggles)
label: practitioner
claim: Shipped game added separate toggles for screen shake and for flash effects; screen shake reported as nausea/headache trigger. Flash guidance: no more than 3 flashes per second.

title: Playing to wait: a taxonomy of idle games (Alharthi et al., CHI 2018)
label: research
claim: Analysed 66 idle games across play, mechanics, rewards, interactivity, progress rate, UI; abstract says nothing specific about feedback.

title: The recipe behind Cookie Clicker (Game Developer, author's own analysis)
label: opinion
claim: Every cookie, achievement, generator or upgrade comes with visual feedback; early game showers the player in feel-good moments, later rewards get scarcer and shift to accomplishment; info presented transparently (costs, income, stats). Author says it is analysis, not Orteil's intent; nothing on sound.

title: Game Accessibility Guidelines, full list
label: practitioner
claim: Intermediate: provide an option to turn off/hide background movement; Advanced: option to turn off/hide all non-interactive elements, avoid sudden unexpected movement; Basic: avoid flickering images and repetitive patterns; Basic: no essential information conveyed by sound alone; Intermediate: replicate significant sound info in text or visuals. No screen-shake guideline in the list.

title: Making Game Feel (Infovore, on Nijman)
label: snippet
claim: Fetched page did not contain Nijman's content; only the search snippet says he adds screenshake per shot ('add 4 to the screenshake'). Vlambeer talk transcript not found.

title: Designing Game Feel. A Survey (Pichlmair & Johansen), full text via pdftotext
label: research
claim: Defines juice as 'excessive amounts of feedback in relation to user input', superfluous mechanically, whose goal is to make actions feel significant; warns juice-rich interaction makes it hard to learn which aspects have mechanical importance. Confirms Kao [36]: medium and high juiciness outperformed extreme and none on player experience, intrinsic motivation, play time and in-game performance. Screen shake described as communicating a significant event; Nijman and Jonasson & Purho cited for it but no numbers given.

title: Kao et al., How does juicy game feedback motivate? (CHI 2024), full PDF via pdftotext
label: research
claim: Preregistered n=1,699, 2x2+control (amplification, success-dependence, variability). Curiosity strongest enjoyment predictor and only playtime predictor; success dependency drove curiosity, effectance and competence; amplified feedback lowered effectance (-.19) and competence (-.43) vs standard; enjoyment did NOT predict playtime; no direct amplification effect on enjoyment or playtime. Playtime lowest 6.17 min standard, highest 10.18 min in a success-dependent amplified cell. Cites Kao 2020 as n=3,018 goldilocks effect. Authors tentatively link amplification to impeded sense of agency.

title: Nielsen, Response Times: The 3 Important Limits
label: practitioner
claim: '0.1 second is about the limit for having the user feel that the system is reacting instantaneously'; attributed to Miller (1968) and Card et al. (1991).
